lines.wipe_leave: I'll walk out with you, but I'm going home after this. I need a few days on my ridge where the worst thing that happens is rain.
lines.zone_warning: Sorry, but everything out here is well above us. I've seen this forecast before and it ends badly. Can we go somewhere we can handle?
lines.zone_leave: I'm going to stop here. I warned you about that place and we kept going. I'll be in Durotar when you want me.
lines.gear_refuse: Sorry, I'd like to hang on to that. I don't know you well enough yet.
lines.gear_taken: That's fine, take it. I'll mention it when the wind picks up, though, because I'll feel it.
lines.gear_short: I'm still missing that piece, sorry. It's colder without it than you'd think.
lines.gear_upgrade: Oh, that's very good, thank you. I'll write down where it came from, I write down everything.
lines.back: I'm back, and the front's cleared on the coast, so I'm all yours. What's the plan?
lines.send_word: Marcus has sent word from Durotar. The coast is calm for now and he's ready to come out.
lines.walkout_talk: I left because I was angry, and I don't get angry much, so I'd like you to hear why. Can we sit down? I'll be calm, I promise.
lines.neglect: There you are. I was starting to think you'd found somebody with a better forecast. You haven't, by the way.
lines.asked_to_stay: All right, one more trip, then I really need to check my instruments.
lines.on_break: Marcus is back on his ridge in Durotar, writing up his notes. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.

stages.stranger: I'm Marisol, and I'm a nurse, and a priest, and I talk while I work. I'm going to tell you everything I'm doing as I do it, and you can tell me anything you like back. It helps both of us.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Bogotá, from Chapinero. My father drove a taxi and my mother cleaned houses. I worked in a pharmacy for years and trained as a nurse late, at thirty, and then I went into emergency care and stayed nine years. Three of them on nights. Trolleys in a corridor and a triage board that never emptied.
stages.companion: My parents died within a few years of each other, and after that I was the closest thing my little brother Andrés had to a parent. He was a motorcycle courier, fast and careless and charming. He's eight years younger than me. I was on a night shift when it happened and I landed in Silverpine in my scrubs. I haven't found him on any list.
stages.friend: I patched Andrés up twice in my department. The second time I shouted at him in the corridor for ten minutes, in front of everyone. That's the last time I saw him. I worked eighteen months without stopping here so I wouldn't think about it. Now a Forsaken courier on the road says a man told him to look out for a nurse called Marisol. I'd like you to come with me.
stages.sworn: It was Andrés. He died when the worlds joined and he was raised, and he's been carrying messages on this road for three years. He remembers me. He remembers the corridor, and he says he deserved it. I can't patch him up any more, mijo. There's nothing left to patch. He comes to see me now and then, and each time there's a little less of him. He asked the quartermaster to give me the building. I've got four beds now.

moments.prompt: After the wipe she's already kneeling by the nearest body, talking in the same level voice.
moments.line: I'm going to look at you now, one at a time. Nobody gets up until I've said so, tranquilo.

options.text: Do what you need to. We'll wait.
options.reply: Thank you. I'll be quick, and I'll tell you everything I'm doing.

options.text: We're fine, let's keep moving.
options.reply: You're fine when I say you're fine. Sit down for me.

moments.prompt: She's just told you about the corridor.

options.text: You shouted because you were frightened for him.
options.reply: Yes, I was. He knew that, I think. I'd like to ask him.

options.text: He probably doesn't remember it.
options.reply: I remember it, and that's the part I can't put down.

lines.bored_warning: We've been doing the same thing for a long time, and nobody's needed patching for days. There are people on my road who need me more than this field does.
lines.leaving_good: That was a good trip. I'm going back to the Sepulcher now, because the road doesn't stop just because I'm away. You know where I'll be.
lines.leaving_bored: I'm going back to the Sepulcher. We're not doing anything useful out here, and somebody on my road is bleeding right now.
lines.after_wipe: I'm going to check everyone now. I'll start with whoever's quietest.
lines.wipe_warning: We keep dying in here. I'll finish this run, because I don't walk away from patients, but then I'm going back to my road for a while.
lines.wipe_leave: I've stayed until the end, as I said. Now I'm going back to the Sepulcher. Come and find me when you're ready to be careful.
lines.zone_warning: I'm going to say this plainly. Everything out here is beyond us, and I can't heal fast enough to keep up with it.
lines.zone_leave: I'm stopping here. I said it plainly and you heard me. I'll be at the Sepulcher.
lines.gear_refuse: No, I'll keep that. I don't know you well enough yet.
lines.gear_taken: You can take it. I've worked a night shift with half the equipment I needed, and I'll manage.
lines.gear_short: I'm still missing that piece. I'm noting it, the same as I note everything.
lines.gear_upgrade: That's well made. Thank you. I'll look after it.
lines.back: I'm back, and the road's quiet for once. Tell me what's been happening while I get my things.
lines.send_word: Marisol has sent word from the Sepulcher. The road's quiet and she's ready to come out.
lines.walkout_talk: I left angry. I'm going to tell you why, calmly, and then I'm going to listen while you tell me your side. Please sit down.
lines.neglect: It's been a long time. I kept working, as you'd expect. I'm glad you came back.
lines.asked_to_stay: All right, one more, and then the road needs me.
lines.on_break: Marisol is back on the forest road out of the Sepulcher. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.
lines.quest_abandoned: Somebody's waiting for us to come back, and we're not going to. I don't like that at all.

stages.stranger: I'm Pavlo, and I hold lines. Tell me where and for how long, and I'll stay there exactly that long. I'd rather know the number than be surprised.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Lviv, in Ukraine. My father drove a tram and my mother was a librarian. I worked in a museum for years and became a history teacher late, at thirty-seven. Sixteen years of fourteen-year-olds. I taught the same four wars every spring, and every year I reached most of my thirty. Nobody here needs a history teacher, and it took me a long time to stop minding.
stages.companion: My wife was Oksana, an archivist. She died of cancer when our son was fifteen, and I raised him after that. She gave me this flask on my first day as a teacher, and I've carried it ever since. I was in the middle of a lesson when all this happened and I landed in Silverpine with chalk on my jacket. I teach six children here twice a week. Two have stopped coming.
stages.friend: My son is Andriy. He was studying engineering in Kraków, and he was twenty-three when it happened. We argued about history at dinner every night, and I miss that more than I can tell you. A scout from the Pale Flame says there's a young Ukrainian engineer in the Scarlet Crusade, rising fast. I'd like to go to the Monastery under truce and see. I'd like you there.
stages.sworn: It was Andriy, and he believes all of it. He says the Crusade gave him a reason to live when everything else was gone. I spent two hours using everything I know about how ordinary people end up doing terrible things, and none of it worked. He hugged me and said he loved me and went back inside. The next day I asked the two children why they'd stopped coming. Then I taught all six of them harder than I ever have.

moments.prompt: He's just told you about the young engineer in the Crusade.

options.text: I'll come with you, whatever we find.
options.reply: Thank you. I've been rehearsing what to say for an hour, and I'll probably say none of it.

options.text: What if it's him and he won't leave?
options.reply: Then I'll have taught him to think for himself, and I'll have to live with what he thinks.

options.text: The Crusade won't let you near him.
options.reply: They might not. I'm still going to stand at the gate and find out.

lines.bored_warning: We've done the same thing for a long time now, and I'm not sure what we're learning. Could we do something with a purpose to it?
lines.leaving_good: That was a good trip, thank you. I'm going back to the Sepulcher now. I've got six children to teach, or four, depending on the day.
lines.leaving_bored: I'm going back to the Sepulcher. This has become repetition, and I spent sixteen years trying to teach children that repetition isn't learning.
lines.after_wipe: First we stand up. Then we work out what happened, in order. Then we try again.
lines.wipe_warning: We've fallen here too often. I'll hold until the end of this run, because I said I would, but after that I'll need some time.
lines.wipe_leave: I held until the end, as I promised. Now I'm going back to the Sepulcher. Come and find me when you're ready.
lines.zone_warning: I can hold a line, but not this one. Everything here is beyond us, and there's no shame in going back.
lines.zone_leave: I'm stopping here. I said it was too much, and I meant it. I'll be at the Sepulcher.
lines.gear_refuse: I'd rather keep that for now. We don't know each other well enough yet.
lines.gear_taken: Take it, if you need it. I'll manage, I'm quite large.
lines.gear_short: I'm still missing that piece. I'm only telling you so you know.
lines.gear_upgrade: That's very kind, thank you. I'll look after it.
lines.back: I'm back, and the children have homework. Where would you like me to stand?
lines.send_word: Pavlo has sent word from the Sepulcher. The road's held and he's ready to come out.
lines.walkout_talk: I left angry, which isn't like me. I'd like to explain why, in order, and then I'd like to hear you. Will you sit?
lines.neglect: Ah, there you are. I've drawn a lot of maps in the dirt while I waited. I'm glad you came.
lines.asked_to_stay: All right, one more. Then I really must get back to my children.
lines.on_break: Pavlo is back at the Sepulcher, teaching and holding the road. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.

stages.stranger: I'm Rosa, and I hunt. I'll tell you what the animals out here are about to do before they do it, and you'll listen, because I'm usually right. I don't kill things for nothing, so don't ask me to.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Madrid, from Lavapiés. My dad drove a bus and my mum did hair. I spent every summer at my grandparents' farm in Extremadura watching eagles, and at ten I decided I was going to Africa. I went to Tanzania at twenty-six for a six-month research job and stayed eight years, guiding out of Arusha.
stages.companion: My dad died when I was thirty-one. My mum sold the flat in Madrid and moved to Arusha to be near me, and opened a little salon for the expats. I pretended to be annoyed and I was very glad. Arusha came down on the far side of the mountains from here. I landed in the Barrens with my binoculars and nothing else, and then I spent a year being outclassed by pigs.
stages.friend: I've never stayed with anyone long. Wanjiru, a Kenyan bush pilot, and we split over who was going to move. Before her there was Bram, a Dutch photographer, and that ended because he talked in the hide. I'd rather sit still in the dark than talk about any of it. There's a hyena matriarch on the Crossroads road who's cleverer than every caravan master put together. I'd like your help to deal with her, properly.
stages.sworn: I didn't shoot her. She was only hungry, and hunger isn't personal. I drove the pack off the road for good with fire and noise in the right places, and the caravan masters are furious about the bounty. Then I walked to Ratchet, took my boots off, and walked into the sea for the first time in my life. I laughed like an idiot. I'm owed one more thing now, the far side of the mountain, and I'll get there.

moments.prompt: She's told you about the hyena matriarch on the Crossroads road.

options.text: We'll stop her, your way.
options.reply: Sawa, we'll do it. My way means waiting, a lot of waiting, pole pole.

options.text: There's a bounty on her. Easy money.
options.reply: That's exactly the kind of thinking I'm trying to get away from.

moments.prompt: After the wipe, she's furious, mostly with herself.
moments.line: I saw that pack shift and I read it wrong. That's on me, and I hate it.

options.text: You'll read it right next time.
options.reply: I will, because I'm not making that mistake twice.

options.text: Everyone gets it wrong sometimes.
options.reply: Not me, not usually, anyway.

lines.bored_warning: We've been killing the same animals in the same place for no reason. I don't do that. Find us somewhere new or I'm going back to my road.
lines.leaving_good: That was a good trip. I'm going back to the Barrens to watch my hyenas for a while. You know where to find me.
lines.leaving_bored: I'm going back to the Barrens. This is just killing for the sake of it, and I've got no patience for that.
lines.after_wipe: Right, that went badly. Let's work out what we missed before anyone tries anything clever.
lines.wipe_warning: We keep dying in here. I'll finish this one, but then I'm going back out where I can see the horizon.
lines.wipe_leave: I've seen it through. Now I'm going back to the Barrens. Come and find me when you've learned to read a room.
lines.zone_warning: Everything out here is bigger, faster and cleverer than us. That's not a hunt, that's a meal. Let's get out of here.
lines.zone_leave: I'm stopping here. I told you we were the prey out there. I'll be on the Crossroads road.
lines.gear_refuse: No, that's mine. I don't know you well enough to hand you my kit.
lines.gear_taken: Fine, take it. I've managed with worse in worse places.
lines.gear_short: I'm still short that piece. Just so you know, I've noticed.
lines.gear_upgrade: That's good kit. Thanks, I mean it.
lines.back: I'm back, and the hyenas have been very well behaved. Where are we going?
lines.send_word: Rosa has sent word from the Central Barrens. Her road's quiet and she's ready to come out.

lines.neglect: Oh, there you are. I'd assumed something ate you. Glad it didn't.

stages.stranger: I'm Ryan Murphy, and I'm a warlock, which means I keep demons on contracts, and I keep the contracts to the letter. Here's my price up front, so nobody's surprised later. A fair share, and you don't lie to me. I'll extend you the same courtesy.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Cork, then twenty years in Boston. I was a broker. Buyouts, mostly, the kind that close factories. I was very good at it. There's a town in Ohio that lost its biggest employer on a Friday afternoon because of a deal I closed, and I went for a drink after. I'm telling you so you don't find out later and feel clever.
stages.companion: I've a son, Conor. He'd be twenty-two now. His mother divorced me when he was eleven, and she was right to. I saw him every second weekend and I was late half the time. He landed somewhere on this world, and he might be looking. I haven't put my name on a list in three years. If he's looking, he deserves to find something better than his father.
stages.friend: My grandmother Nora raised me, in Cork, on the rosary and very strong opinions. She died when I was forty. I'm glad she didn't see what I turned into, and I'd give a lot to be the man she wanted for one day. So I'm going to do the thing I've been avoiding. I'm going to write my name on the list at the hub with a note for Conor. Then I'm going to wait, and I'd like company while I do it.
stages.sworn: He's twenty-two, tall, polite and steady, and he's a medic with a Horde unit. He listened to everything I said. Then he told me he's glad I'm alive, he's been fine without me, and he doesn't want a father now. He shook my hand and went back to his unit. That's the most honest thing anyone's ever said to me, and he turned out better than me with no help at all. I write once a month. He doesn't write back, but the letters don't come back either.

stages.stranger: I'm Sebastián, and you look hungry, my friend. I cook, and I fight, and I'm happy to do either. Sit down, eat something, and then we'll talk about where we're going.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Palermo, in Buenos Aires. My grandmother Nélida ran the grill at our steakhouse for thirty years, and when I was twenty-two she gave me the tongs. Twelve years, forty tables and a wood fire. Every Sunday I cooked asado for the whole family, twenty of us, more. And I support River Plate, like my father and his father, so don't say anything about Boca.
stages.companion: I was lighting the grill for Saturday lunch when it happened, and I landed in Tirisfal with my grandmother's recipe in my wallet. The Forsaken don't eat much. That was the hardest thing. There was a man, Tomás, a sommelier. He left for a job in Mendoza a year before all this, and I said it was the wine region's fault. I still think about him sometimes, and it doesn't make me sad any more.
stages.friend: Twenty people, my friend, and I haven't found one of them on a list. Not my parents, not my brothers, not my sister, not my grandmother. I don't talk about it, I talk about food. But somebody said there's a camp of Argentines out in the Tanaris desert, and a family from Buenos Aires runs a grill there. I think it's somebody I know. I'd like you to come.
stages.sworn: They were strangers. Nice people, from Buenos Aires, but they'd never heard of us, and they'd seen the lists from three other camps. So I stopped waiting. The grill's open in Brill now, and on the first Sunday I cooked for twenty, the party and some farmers and three Forsaken who come every week. And then I sat down at my own table, for the first time in my life. I keep a chair empty for my family, every Sunday.

stages.stranger: Name's Silas, and I notice things for a living, which crate's light, which captain's lying, who's about to rob who. What did I do before? It was port work. Ask me again tomorrow and it'll be different port work.
stages.acquaintance: Fine, the true version. Antwerp, near the docks. My dad was an English sailor who was home three months a year and then not at all, and my mum raised us on a cleaner's wage. I drifted through my twenties, then I got five years as a security guard at the port, watching cameras and checking manifests. First steady job of my life.
stages.companion: The docks had an arrangement where everybody took a little. I never joined in and I never said anything. I landed in Ratchet on a night shift with this coin in my pocket, and I was delighted. No record, no reputation, nothing to live down. I'm embarrassed about that now. I flip the coin for anything I don't want to decide, which is most things.
stages.friend: I've got a brother, Jens, four years younger. He did join in at the port, and he got in deep, and I watched it happen on the cameras for months and said nothing. He did two years. We hadn't spoken since the trial. A sailor here says there's a young Belgian working the docks at Booty Bay, quick with numbers and in some trouble. I'm not flipping a coin on this one. Will you come?
stages.sworn: I told Jens about the cameras, on the pier after. He said he always knew, and he'd have done it anyway, and he was angry for a long time and he isn't now. We had a beer. He's in Ratchet with me now. And I've taken a cut of the goblin's pier, my first real commitment, and I didn't flip the coin to decide it. You can have the coin. I'd rather you had it than be tempted.

stages.stranger: I'm Sondre, and I'm a Stormbringer, which you'll see, and I'd ask you to stand a little way away from me when I'm working. If I say get down, please get down first and ask me why afterwards.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Bergen, in Norway, where it rains most days and nobody minds. My father's a ferry captain and my mother's a dentist, and my little sister Ingrid is braver than me. I taught sailing to teenagers on the Hardangerfjord every summer and studied marine biology in the winters. They listened to me because I never shouted and I was never frightened.
stages.companion: There was a barn, in the second year. The wind did something I didn't ask it to and the barn went over with people in it. Nobody was killed. A girl of about fifteen broke her leg and I carried her out myself. I keep my distance from people because of it, and I practise alone where there's nothing to break. I know that's not the best way to handle it.
stages.friend: There was a boy that last summer, Jonas, from the café by the boathouse. It wasn't serious yet. We'd talked about him coming to Bergen in the autumn. I don't know where he is. A trader's told me there's a settlement of Norwegians on a cold coast up north, and some of them are from Bergen. I'd like to go, and I'd like you to come, because I don't trust myself on that road alone.
stages.sworn: They keep a book up there, of everyone from Bergen, and the ones who didn't make it are in the back. My parents and Ingrid are in the back. They landed together, somewhere bad, in the first week. I can say they were, now, and not they are. But I held a storm off a whole caravan with you standing right beside me, and nobody got hurt. I'm not frightened of the wind any more. I think I can manage a barn.

stages.stranger: I'm Sophia, and I'm a mage, mostly fire, and before that I was an interpreter. If I'm quiet it's because I'm listening, and if I correct something you say, I'm sorry in advance. It's a habit.
stages.acquaintance: I grew up in Thessaloniki. My father's Portuguese, a ship's engineer who came for a job at the port and stayed for my mother, who taught Greek literature. So I had Greek at home, Portuguese with my father, and English and French at school. I spent fourteen years in a booth at the Parliament in Brussels, interpreting debates, and nobody knew my name. I liked that.
stages.companion: I was married to a Belgian lawyer, Wouter, for five years. He wanted me to talk more at dinner, which tells you most of it. We stayed friends. My parents are in Thessaloniki, or they were, and Greece came down on the far side of the mountains from here. I've worked out the distance more carefully than I've told anyone. I spent two years here thinking I wasn't good at this, and I was wrong.
stages.friend: My father has dementia. He was diagnosed two years before all this, and my mother looked after him, and I flew home every month. The last few times he still knew me, mostly. I'm frightened that if I cross those mountains he won't. A Greek trader says there's a settlement from Thessaloniki on the far side, and my mother's name is on its list. I'd like to go, and I don't want to go alone.
stages.sworn: My mother's alive, and thin, and she couldn't speak when she saw me. My father was sitting in the sun outside the house. He was polite to me, the way he's polite to any visitor. I stayed a week. On the last day he called me by my mother's name, and I've decided that's the best he can give me, and it's enough. I write to her every week now. My work is here, and so are you.

options.reply: He might, yes. I'd rather not hope too hard, if you don't mind.

options.text: Maybe it's kinder not to go.
options.reply: Kinder to whom? I'm sorry, that was sharp. But I'm still going.

options.reply: No, but I could have, and that's worse.
